North America refrigerates eggs because they are washed at the farm. Washing has the benefit of immediately removing potential contaminants but has the side effect of removing the natural protective coating so the egg becomes more susceptible to contanimation from that point on (ergo they need to be refrigerated after washing). Unwashed eggs maintain their natural protective coating and tend not to need refrigeration however they may still harbour pathogens on the shell.

Note, if you do wash an egg you must use hot water. Cold water can cause the internals to contract and actually pull contanimants through the shell.

I'm dual-boot with Ubuntu and Win7. Is there a way to delete the Windows partition and add it to the Ubuntu partition without losing data or screwing up grub?

Yes. But it'd be simpler and safer to just leave it as a separate partition, but mount it under linux. You can mount it anywhere in the directory tree, so you could probably find somewhere where its size would fit well. I always use different partitions for system, home, and a storage dump directory.

But if you really want it all joined to an existing partition you can delete the windows partition entirely, then use parted to resize the Linux partition. It can do it without (probably) harming the existing Linux data.
That does require that the partitions are beside each other in the table, or that you can destroy all partitions between them.

It can do it without (probably) harming the existing Linux data. That does require that the partitions are beside each other in the table, or that you can destroy all partitions between them.

If it is possible depends on the file system. If the partitions aren't next to each other, you make a software RAID0, but that's a lot of work and breaking grub is likely.

Reformatting the windows partition and mounting it is the easy and safe way. Otherwise I'd recommend a full backup. But if you do a full backup anyway, why not repartition your drive and restore the backup?

My disk looks like this (in order):

/dev/sda1 Recovery

/dev/sda2 NTFS

/dev/sda3 Extended partition (Ubuntu)

You can do it then. You could delete sda2 and add it to sda3, or delete both sda1 and sda2 and add them both.
There is always a warning that it could lose data, but I've never personally had it fail.

The only thing that might bite you on this, assuming the resize goes off without a hitch, is that sda3 will become sda1 after you delete the other partitions. If your bootloader and fstab are referencing root by UUID, which is the standard these days, then you should be fine; if they're not, though, you'll have to go into single user mode and change the pointers accordingly.

As others have said, GParted should probably do it just fine. I'd like to add however that deleting a partition that is in front of the Ubuntu partition will likely mess grub up. Be prepared with a boot-repair disk.
